I wish to direct the attention of the house to a matter concerning the privileges of all members, irrespective of group or party. I read in this morning's Citizen the following message, transmitted by the Canadian press:
Toronto, March 11.-General dissatisfaction *was voiced here to-night respecting the fate of the Ontario Divorce Court bill on its second reading in the House of Commons to-night, by those who had shown interest in its passage.
G. McLaughlin, secretary of the County of York La\v Association, said it was "much to be regretted" that the vote had resulted as it did, but added he had expected far stronger opposition.
"It is unfortunate that Quebec is so solidly against a matter which Ontario seems to favour, and unfortunate that Quebec can determine whether or not Ontario will have divorce courts," said W. J. McCullum, president of the association.
I also find this despatch from Brantford, Ontario, dated March 11:
Commenting on the defeat to-night of the Ontario Divorce Court bill in the House of Commons, W. J. Carson, newly-elected grand master of the Royal Black Chapter, Loyal Orange Lodge, said:
"We don't agree with the principle of the action-.that French Canadians of Quebec province should be in a position to say that Ontario shall or shall not have a divorce court-to dictate the policies of a sister province when the British North America Act provides that responsible machinery of the courts shall be under the control of the province in which those courts are located.
"Ontario does not interfere with Quebec or her code."
There are a few minor points in that despatch to which exception could be taken, but I am not going to discuss them. I have made a count of the votes as recorded in Hansard at page 522, and I find that out of the 78 votes recorded in favour of the bill-

This is no question of
privilege, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member is simply answering someone who has made an observation outside this house altogether. That has absolutely nothing to do with the members of this house.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends may laugh, but the point is this, that an hon. member is taking advantage of the rule of this house which permits him or any other member to contradict anything affecting his honour or questioning his conduct that appears in the press. He has taken advantage of that rule for the purpose of asserting what some gentleman said outside with regard to his opinions in this house.
What objection have you to its being contradicted?

I have none, but he has
a place outside the house where he can contradict it, and I object to the rules of the house being used for that purpose, if we or others affected are not allowed to reply to him.

My sole object, Mr. Speaker, is precisely to assert the privileges of this house, to assert the liberty of members voting as they please. Nobody is questioning that.

Privilege-Mr. Neill

Bourinot says at page
303:
la the Canadian house, questions of privilege take a wide range, but it may be stated in general terms that they refer to all matters affecting the rights and immunities of the house collectively, or to the position and conduct of members in their representative character.
I gather from the extracts read by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) that he is simply explaining the attitude taken by himself and some other members, which attitude he feels has been misrepresented in the press.

Mr. Speaker, I am not
going to discuss at all the issue raised yesterday. I simply wish to point out that having counted the votes in yesterday's division, I find that out of the seventy-eight votes recorded in support of the motion of my friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth), twenty-three votes were given by Ontario members in favour of the second reading of the bill, and that twenty-six votes were recorded against the second reading by members elected by Ontario constituencies. With the help of that handy book, the Parliamentary Companion, I found further that of those twenty-six Ontario votes recorded against the second reading of the bill, there were thirteen Liberals and thirteen Conservatives. I well remember the old days when there was talk of "The noble thirteen." Well, this time both parties can claim the honour of having in their ranks a "noble thirteen."
So it amounts to this, that, supposing the whole of the membership representing Quebec constituencies had abstained from voting one way or the other, the bill proposed by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre would have imposed upon Ontario, as against the expressed wish of the majority of the Ontario members of this house, a matter which apparently the membership from Ontario, Conservative and Liberal alike, do not want to have. If the members for Quebec are going to be taken to task in papers published in Ontario or elsewhere for giving a free vote one way or the other, because it happens not to please certain people, what may be said of the members from the western provinces in endeavouring to impose a divorce court on the province of Ontario against the expressed will of the representatives of Ontario in this house?
But, sir, claiming for all the members of parliament as for myself, irrespective of creed, race, province or party, the basic principle of British fair play, justice and government, I claim that every man has a right to vote as he thinks and as he wants to. I acknowledge to our friends from the western provinces the
undoubted right to have voted as they did, and I claim for myself and my fellow members from Quebec the same right, without being branded over the province of Ontario as endeavouring to impose upon that province something that it does not want. I leave it to the conscience and the free judgment of all members of this house, irrespective of creed, party or province, whether it is not a basic principle of this house that we should have the right to vote as we please upon any ques tion which comes before us.
PRIVILEGE-Mr. NEILL

Mr. Speaker, I rise also to a question of privilege. On page 485 of Hansard is to be found a statement by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) which I wish to correct. His statement reads as followss-he was speaking of myself:
Let me quote a few of his words, in 1926, when he moved a resolution respecting grading of eggs, to see how he stands. He evidently was in favour of the wording of the agreement, hut he did not want to vote against the government. I will just take his own words for it. He said:
I will not proceed further with the quotation. He then quoted a few sentences beginning in the middle of a paragraph by which, diverted from what went before and from the context, he sought to prove I said or meant something not only entirely different from but the exact opposite of what a perusal of my speech or even of the paragraph itself would show. I may say that I was not moving a resolution against the grading of eggs, I was speaking against an amendment as a vote of want of confidence proposing to do away with the grading of eggs. I specifically stated that on that and other occasions I had wanted to vote against the government, but I could not do it on this particular amendment as I believed in the grading of eggs. What I said will be found at page 4177 of Hansard of 1926. I think such misrepresentation, sir, is unworthy of the member.
Any more privilege?

I should say that at least one or two questions might well be raised as to privilege. The last observation made by the hon. member that " such misrepresentation was unworthy of the members," is certainly not a question of privilege.
It ought to be expunged from Hansard.

1.	Has the government any plans for providing useful employment for the great body of the unemployed?
2.	If so, what relief will be afforded?
3.	Will the government accept the offer of the province of Ontario to provide one-third of the cost of certain forms of relief in conjunction with the federal and municipal authority?

1,	2, 3. With a view to affording employment, the federal government has authorized its several departments to carry on, during periods of seasonal unemployment, work or construction which ordinarily, because of extra cost involved, would not be carried on until a more favourable season, and is prepared to meet in its entirety the extra cost of work carried on under federal authority, at additional cost during such time, without requesting either the provinces or municipalities to provide one-third each of such additional cost. In these circumstances it is assumed that the provinces and municipalities will in like manner meet any additional expenditures incurred by them on provincial and municipal works constructed for like purposes. The federal government has also, as a means of avoiding unemployment, authorized its departments to continue in employment, so far as may reasonably be possible, where their services can be utilized, employees whose services on strictly business grounds might be temporarily disposed of during periods of seasonal unemployment. The government has also caused it to be known that it will view with favour the extension of this policy to undertakings in the nature of government owned utilities or projects assisted by public funds.

Mr. Speaker, much to my regret I find that I must ask the house to reject the motion presented by the hon. member for Southeast Grey. Its adoption would be contrary to the rule that has been in force in England for many years and in Canada ever since the days of Sir John Thompson as Minister of Justice. The question apparently did not arise before that date because up to that time the exercise of clemency was practically limited to capital cases. Since Sir John Thompson's time, however, his successors in office, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick (Hansard, March 1, 1905, p. 1849), Sir Allen Aylesworth, Right Honourable Charles Doherty (Hansard, May 29, 1917, p. 1814), and Sir Lomer Gouin (Hansard, April 18, 1923, p. 1975), have all maintained that documents relating to an exercise of clemency should be treated as confidential and that it would not be proper nor advisable to make them public. Sir Wilfrid Laurier as leader of the government on one occasion and as leader of the opposition at a later date also supported this view. The English practice is set forth by Todd: a quotation from that author's Parliamentary Government in England seems to cover the whole question:
No interference by either house of parliament with the exercise of this prerogative is justifiable, except under extraordinary circumstances. It was said by Macaulay, that he would rather entrust it to the hands of the very worst ministry that ever held office than allow it to be exercised under the direction of the very best House of Commons; and by Sir Robert Peel, that he would leave this prerogative in the hands of the executive considering that it was the right and duty of the house to interfere only if there be a suspicion that justice is perverted for corrupt purposes.
In the case before us Mr. Speaker, which I have carefully examined, I find there is nothing to justify me in making an exception to the general practice. I would, therefore ask my hon. friend not to press the motion.
Motion negatived.

Before I call notices of
motion, in deference to the house I wish to declare that owing to a clerical error I cast my vote last evening on the bill moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). As there was no tie that vote ought to be invalidated.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the estimates should be referred to select standing committees before being submitted to the committee of the whole.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, unlike some of the
resolutions which have come before this house at this session-and which have been opposed by the governemnt because their adoption would have caused a further drain on the treasury-I should like to say that the adop tion of the resolution which I am introducing this afternoon should be welcomed bj the administration, because it has for its purpose a further safeguarding of the treasury and a saving in the time of the house. It is not my intention to debate this question at any great length; it already has been before the house on several occasions, but for one reason or another, the house never has had the opportunity of pronouncing upon it.
I find that you, Mr. Speaker, introduced a similar resolution in the session of 1921, and at that time you very ably and eloquently placed before the members of the house good and sufficient reasons why this resolution should have been adopted. I find also that on that occasion you were well supported by the present Prime Minister, who was then leader of the Liberal party in opposition. The resolution, however, did not come to a vote, as it was withdrawn.
It was introduced again in the session of 1925 by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), but was shelved on that occasion because of an amendment which was introduced referring it to the committee of the house then sitting on the revision of the rules of the house. The report of the committee will be found in the Journals of the house, 1925, at page 360:
Your committee is of the opinion that the question of referring estimates to special committees before being submitted to the committee of supply is one of great importance which.

Rules of the House-Mr. Lucas
does not come entirely within the scope of a committee appointed to revise the rules, and it recommends that the same be considered by a special committee at the next session of parliament.
Nothing further was heard of this question until late in the session of 1928 when, on a motion to go into supply, the leader of the opposition moved an amendment condemning the expenditures of the government as excessive and extravagant. This was regarded by the government as a vote of want of confidence, and in speaking to this amendment the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) intimated that unless we had some assurance that provision would be made whereby we might be able to scrutinize these estimates in a more businesslike manner, the possibilities were that this corner of the house might support that amendment. Speaking in that debate the hon. member is reported as follows:
For several years we have pressed from this section of the assembly that there ought to be a better method of examining the expenditures of the country. We have asked from time to time that estimates be either allocated to various standing committees of the house, or that special committees be appointed to attend to this matter. So far we have not received much encouragement.
A little further on he stated:
But I do insist that the government give us now some assurance that at subsequent sessions an attempt will be made to deal a little more efficiently with the examination of the expenditures of the country.
Following the remarks of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, the Prime Minister is reported at page 4048, revised edition of Hansard, 1928, as follows:
I entirely agree with my hon. friend that the system at present in force, under which a minister of the crown is necessarily dependent in the House of Commons on his deputy for much of the needed information with the deputy, also of necessity, often not wholly familiar with all the details of particular branches, is most unsatisfactory. Speaking for the government I would say that we would welcome a change in the present method, a change which would not only afford fuller opportunity for discussion but which would carry with it an obligation on the part of the heads of different branches of the public service to appear before a committee of the house and explain fully the reasons which have occasioned the recommendations which find their place in the estimates submitted to the house.
Having said this I would like to supplement my remarks further by saying that if we are not voted out of office as a result of this blanket amendment and if when another session comes around we still retain the confidence of the House of Commons, one of the first matters to which we will ask the house to give its attention and consideration will be

the one mentioned by my hon. friend, namely that of arranging some method by which the estimates may to a greater or less extent be considered by a special committee or by the standing committees of the house.
At the last session of parliament another resolution was introduced by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), but when the resolution was reached it was ruled out of order, because this matter had been already referred to the select standing committee on standing orders. Early last session the Prime Minister, true to his promise, made the following motion, which is to be found at page 48 of the Journals of the house, 1929:
Mr. Mackenzie King (Prince Albert) moved: That the select standing committee on standing orders be instructed to consider the advisability of amending the standing orders so that certain estimates may be referred to a committee and so that bills reported from a standing or select committee shall be placed on the order paper for third reading after having been sufficiently debated by the house.
You will note that the last part of this motion is a certain form of closure when dealing with the third reading of bills.
When the right hon. Prime Minister made this motion the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) took exception, and referred to it as a double-barrelled motion, as it later proved to be. The select standing committee on standing orders reported on this matter, and their report is to be found at page 78, of the Journals of the house, 1929:
Your committee recommend that, during the present session, the house may refer any of the estimates to a standing or special committee, concurrently with the committee of supply, but that none of the estimates shall be concurred in by the house until reported by the committee of supply.
Your committee further recommends that, during the present session, when any bill, other than a government bill, reported from any standing or special committee, shall have been considered at two sittings and not disposed of, it shall be placed on the order paper for third reading; and when called in pursuance thereof, the question "That the bill be now read a third time" shall be put by Mr. Speaker and decided without debate or amendment.
The trouble we found with this report was that it dealt with two questions, which caused the hon. member for Acadia to term it a double-barrelled motion, the second barrel dealing with third reading of bills and when it came before the house hon. members found that in order to get what they wanted they were compelled to vote for something they did not want, a system of closure on the third reading of bills, which proved very objectionable to a great many members. When this report was brought before the house for concurrence the hon. member for Comox-

Rules of the House-Mr. Mackenzie King
Alberni (Mr. Neill) moved the adjournment of the debate, so that the house up to the present time never has had the opportunity of dealing with it. That motion remained on the order paper during the whole of last session.
I think it is recognized by every hon. member of the house that the present system of dealing with the estimates is far from satisfactory. With our tremendous debt and our annual expenditure continually growing, anything that will enable hon. members to vote supply in a more intelligent and businesslike way, so as to take care of the needs of an expanding country, should be welcomed by all parties in the house. It is estimated that two-thirds of our expenditures are uncontrolled, which is all the more reason why we should give the very closest scrutiny to the small portion over which we have control. I believe that the adoption of the resolution which I have introduced this afternoon will not only effect an economy in expenditure but it will effect also an economy in the time of the house. It would affect also the expenditures made for political purposes. We know that charges are made nearly every session that certain expenditures are made for political reasons, and no matter which party was in power, I feel sure that if the ministers in charge knew that their estimates were to go before a special committee they would be very careful about placing in those estimates anything of a political nature.
In fairness to the ministers, it cannot be expected that they will have all the details of the estimates at their finger tips. At times when a minister has not been able to give a complete answer some hon. member has intimated that he is withholding information and that there is some political motive for that action, and the result at times has been that we get into a very long and tedious debate which consumes the time of the house. Very often an hon. member will ask a question and before a reply is given another hon. member will ask another with the result that the first question is forgotten and has to be repeated. Under our present system at times an hon. member is compelled to vote upon an item for which he assumes responsibility without having full information regarding the same.
The procedure which I propose has worked very satisfactorily in connection with the estimates for the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian National Steamships. The officers of the department are present in the committee and those estimates are threshed out in a free and open manner, and considerable time is saved in the house when the 2419-34
estimates come up for consideration by the committee of the whole. The same result would obtain with the estimates of other departments. Members of the house could appear before the committee where the officers and engineers of the department would be present to give full and complete information. In that way the members would be more fully informed when the estimates came before the committee of the whole, and the estimates would be passed with a great saving of time. As members of parliament we are trustees of the people's money but under our present system we do not have the information to enable us to vote intelligently upon matters concerning expenditures for which they have to assume responsibility.
Speaking personally as a prairie member, I know very little about the needs and requirements for breakwaters and wharves and such things in the maritime provinces. We find large sums of money voted in the estimates each year, and at times we wonder whether or not they are required. The information we receive in that regard does not always satisfy our curiosity and I feel sure that if members from the west could interview the engineers and officers of the various departments and thus obtain full and complete details they would be much more satisfied.
As I stated before, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to debate this question at any length. It has been before the house on several occasions and the Prime Minister has stated that he was in favour of the proposal. The select standing committee on standing orders, to which this question was referred, has reported in favour of it and I think that all that remains to be done is for the members of the house to be given an opportunity to pronounce upon it. If that were done I feel quite sure that this resolution would be adopted unanimously.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there does
not seem tc 'be a desire upon the part of many hon. members to participate in this debate. I assume that is due to the fact that a similar resolution has been before the house upon two or three previous occasions, and to all intents and purposes a committee erf the house, though no-t the house itself, has endorsed the principle of this resolution.
As I understand it, the hon. member is interested primarily in having an expression of view from the house as to whether or not certain estimates-I think he will agree to that, rather than all estimates-should be referred either to select standing committees or to a committee appointed especially to deal

530	COMMONS
Rules oj the House-Mr. Mackenzie King
with estimates. I make that suggestion as an alternative because there are some estimates which could not go appropriately to any particular select standing committee. The principle aimed at in the resolution is that the estimates should go before some committee of the house for preliminary discussion and consideration, before which committee officials of the public sendee could be called and .members thereby enabled to obtain more detailed information than is generally possible when the estimates are being discussed in committee of supiply. If that is the desire of my hon. friend, I would say that so far as the government is concerned we are in entire accord with the purpose and spirit of the resolution.
As has been mentioned already by the hon. member, I moved personally on February 15 last year, the following resolution:
That the select standing committee on standing orders be instructed to consider the advisability of amending the standing orders so that certain estimates may be referred to a commitce and so that bills reported from a standing or select committee shall be placed on the order paper for third reading after having been sufficiently debated by the house.
The hon. member has reminded us that at that time some exception was taken to the form of that resolution u,pon the ground that it was double-barrelled. I pointed out that it did deal with two separate subjects, but that the purpose of it was to refer each of those subjects to the select committee and that it did not necessarily follow that the house would have to adopt both of them; it could adopt one or both of the proposals, or reject either or 'both. On February 21 of last year, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Morin), the chairman of the select standing committee on standing orders, presented a report as follows:
Mr. L. S. R. Morin (St. Hyacinthe-Rouville) presented the first report of the select standing committee on standing orders as follows:
And then is quoted the order, and the report continues:
Your committee recommend that, during the present session, the house may refer any of the estimates to a standing or special committee, concurrently with the committee of supply, but that none of the estimates shall be concurred in by the house until reported by the committee of supply.
Then there is a reference to the other barrel of the resolution, and the opinion of the committee is given with respect thereto. That resolution was before the house on February 26, and if I am not mistaken., it was the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) who took a rather strong exception to the recommendation in debate. He pointed out that in his opinion the resolution would restrict the

freedom of members in debate in the house. This was, I believe, the last thing in the mind of anyone who wished to have the estimates go before a committee. Indeed, the purpose was quite the apposite. The hon. member cast a great deal of ridicule on the proposal, and then moved the adjournment of the debate. I have in my hand the orders of the. day of last year and from the 26th February until the last day of the session there stood at the head of routine proceedings the following order:
Resuming the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Morin (St. Hyacinthe-Rouville) for the concurrence in the first report of the select standing committee on standing orders.
It was open to any hon. member at any time from the 26th February until June 14 to move concurrence in that report. If it were not desired to concur in the report in its entirety, an amendment could have been made accepting the portion of the report which hon. members wish to have adopted. The fact that throughout the whole session no single member, though each one was free to make the motion, moved concurrence in the report or in any portion of it led the government to assume that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) had so impressed the house with his speech that no one else wished to take the matter up, and it was allowed to remain in that comatose condition until the end of the session.
Now the matter in so far as it relates to estimates comes forward as a single resolution. If my hon. friend is prepared to make his resolution a little general and for the word " estimates " to insert the words " certain estimates " and to make it read " a special committee or select standing committees " instead of just " select standing committees "-and I think he would be agreeable to doing this-the government would have no objection to having the resolution carried and, in fact, its members would be prepared to support it. I would wish, however, to make perfectly clear that hon. members are free to vote as they please and also note what the government has in mind in having it made possible to refer estimates to a select standing committee, is simply to provide means whereby hon. members can get more in the way of detailed information with respect to the estimates than is generally possible when we are discussing them in the committee of supply. We believe a great deal of time might be saved if estimates went before either select standing committees or a special committee for the purpose and were considered there, but there would have to be the distinct understanding that in no particular was the right of any member

Rules oj the House-Sir George Perley
to discuss any or all of the estimates restricted in any way when they were before the house in committee of supply. I think it should be made quite clear that so far as the committee of supply is concerned, its rights or the activities of any of its members would not be restricted in any particular.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: W ould the Prime Minister amplify the term " certain estimates " so as to indicate what scope that would have?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
It would have just such scope as the house would wish to give. If the house, for example, wished the estimates of the Department of Agriculture to go to the select standing commttee on agriculture, those estimates might be so referred. If it were so desired, the estimates of the Department of External Affairs might be referred to the committee on industrial and international relations, and so on, regard being had to the particular class of estimates to be considered.
I would like my hon. friend to realize that to put into practice the purpose of his resolution would require an amendment to the rules. The government would wish to wait until there was a special committee dealing with amendments to the rules before acting upon the resolution. We recognize that careful thought should be given to the many considerations of which account should be taken in adopting any new practice in parliament. If, however, the house adopts the motion, when the house decides to have a committee to amend the rules, the resolution could be brought immediately to its attention as an opinion of the house with respect to a certain course which should be adopted in dealing with the estimates. It would then be for the committee to make its own recommendation to the house with respect to any necessary changes in procedure.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I
think the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) should receive the thanks of the house for bringing up this question again this year. It is very important and requires a good deal of consideration. Our first duty in parliament is to see that everything, particularly the estimates, is carefully considered. If we start with that idea, anything we can do that will save the time of the house, it seems to me, ought to be adopted.
As regards what happened last session, what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) says is true about the motion which was brought in and which stood on the order paper for a long time. My hon. friend made an error in coupling these two things together 2419-34*
in that motion. They were entirely different and, as the hon. member for Camrose has said, it is quite evident that many hon. members might support one who would be definitely against the other. The Prime Minister suggests that any member could have gone on with the adjourned motion. That is true, but that would bring up the discussion of both these points, and it seems to me the proper way to deal with the matter is to have a motion with regard to this one point only and if the other point should ever be brought up again-and many members think it should not be-then it could be moved as a separate motion.
I am going to make a suggestion which is entirely my own, and that is that this session we should try out this scheme with the estimates of one of the departments. The Department of Public Works has the greatest number of items in the estimates. It is the one as regards which the members would liketly prefer most of all to be able to ask questions of other officials in the department than the minister only to whom the information is given on the floor of the house by the deputy minister. If we could consider the estimates of the Department of Public Works in a committee, that would go a long way toward reducing the time which the house spends on estimates. Certainly, as the Prime Minister has said, we must preserve the right to discuss anything we like when we are in committee of supply, but it seems quite evident to me that if there are in the Department of Public Works, for instance, estimates about which I would like some information, and if I could get that in a committee by asking the deputy minister or other officials, then I am in a position, if I want to bring the matter up in the house, to do so briefly and not to spend a long time getting from the minister information which he very often does not have and which sometimes he is not very willing to give. If we try this scheme this session in regard to the estimates of the Department of Public Works-and I suppose that would mean a special committee-then we would see whether it would work out in the same way as it has done in regard to the estimates of the Canadian National Railways. The estimates of the Canadian National Railways are brought before a special committee and threshed out there very fully. When they come into the house any hon. member has a perfect right to bring up any question in connection with those estimates, but experience has taught us that as a rule not much time is taken up with the estimate* of the Canadian National Railways for the

Rules of the House-Mr. MacLaren
reason that they have been so thoroughly threshed out in committee and the members have had an. opportunity of asking questions of various officials and getting the information. they want.
The Prime Minister says that a motion made to amend the rules would be the proper way to bring this matter up. I would suggest to him that as he is satisfied to have this done, he should make a motion that the committee on standing orders should consider the question and make a report as to the best way of dealing with it. If he approves my suggestion that we try this out this session with regard to the estimates of the Public Works department only, I do not think this requires a change in the rules. The house has the right at any time to appoint a special committee for any purpose it chooses, and if the question were considered by the committee on standing orders and they made a report that the estimates of the Public Works department, if my suggestion is approved, should be taken up in a special committee this session, and that report were concurred in by the house, that would cover the point and the house could name a committee for that purpose. It may not be found to work out as well as some members hope, but if this session we made the experiment with this one department, which has the greatest number of items in the estimates, we would know better what to do about the other departments another year.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
If this proposal were carried into effect, I think that a good deal would be lost. What would be gained would be a saving of the time of the house, because after the estimates had been discussed by the special committee the discussion in the house would be materially shortened. But there are other things more important than the saving of time. When the estimates are first brought before the committee of the whole, general information is given and as a result the members as a whole are much better informed as to the expenditures and accounts than they would be if the estimates were referred to special committees. We have a special committee now to consider the estimates of the Canadian National Railways It is true that the members of that particular committee have obtained an intimate knowledge of the railway accounts, but the House of Commons has lost so far as the information of the members generally is concerned. I think most members know less about the railway accounts now than they did before this arrangement was made.

It. may be said that the estimates may be discussed in the house after coming from the special committee. That is true; they may be discussed, but they will not be. There woidd be a general feeling that having been discussed and disposed of in one committee they should not be discussed again in the house, except in very exceptional eases. The railway estimates for instance, are not much discussed in the house. So far as those estimates are concerned, I think we have saved time by referring them to a special committee, but we have lost in our general information.
There is one other point. Different groups of members are especially interested in the estimates affecting their own portion of the country, and it is their duty to familiarize themselves with them, and to follow them up. But if a member does not happen to be on the special committee, his life would be a burden trying to keep in touch with the committee so that he could attend when particular estimates in which he was interested came up for discussion and hear what was going on. I presume that he would be allowed to take part in the discussion if he requested the privilege. That is a serious practical objection.
Under the present system I believe that all the members are acquiring a vast amount of useful information regarding the country generally. I think that the advantages of the present system outweigh its disadvantages. I think we would lose more than we would gain by changing the present system. We would save time, but we would lose in knowledge. We would lose our opportunity, as representing constituencies, to be present when certain estimates were under discussion by the committee, because there would be great difficulty in keeping in touch with the committee and ascertaining just when those items were coming up.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): I desire to assure my hon friend that while the government, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has stated, is in accord with the general principle of the resolution, it is not desired that the impression should be conveyed that the government is attempting to force this or any other method of dealing with the estimates upon the house. Rather it welcomes the opportunity of discussing such methods as have been suggested 'by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) and by others on previous occasions in previous sessions. Certainly there is some point in what my hon. friend from St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren) says. The one experience

Rules oj the House-Mr. Dunning
we have had in this matter up to the present is with the committee dealing with the Canadian National railway estimates. The evidence taken before that committee has been made a matter of record, and is usually printed and is available, but I agree with my hon. friend that it is not quite so easy to gather from a printed record of evidence what you particularly want to know, as if you were present and could ask particular questions, which may not have been asked in your absence.
I have taken a little trouble, somewhat hurriedly, to find what has 'been the British experience, for after all we can learn what is likely to happen in our own case by studying what has happened in other assemblies similarly situated. I find that in Great Britain the creation of an estimates committee has been discussed for upwards of fifty years. In 1912 such a committee was set up. It did not function at all effectually due to the outbreak of the war, and it was not until 1921 that a general debate on the subject took place in the British House of Commons. On a previous occasion this session I quoted what Sir Austen Chamberlain and Mr. Asquith said on that occasion. In any event the result of that debate was to set up a committee to function under somewhat elaborate regulations. I shall not burden the house with the regulations, ten in number, but they do indicate the necessity of careful study on the part of the select standing committee on standing orders as to the kind of rules under which such committees should function if established in the Canadian House of Commons.
There is, of course, the question that occurs at once to everyone's mind:	If this new
method is adopted, what effect will it have upon the rights of members of the house in committee of supply? I am sure that my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Per-ley) and everyone would agree that nothing that is done by way of a special committee in the examination of estimates should in any way impair the rights of members of the house in committee of supply.
The second point which assumed considerable importance in Great Britain was as to the effect of the new system upon ministerial and departmental responsibility for the preparation and presentation of estimates. Looking through the record of the experience of Great Britain, I find that that question grew more and more important as the years passed, and it is very evident from the British experience that it should be made clear that
such committees on estimates, if appointed, would have no authority to increase the estimates or to report favourably for increases along this or that line.

There is, of course, some difference between our situation in this parliament and the situation in the British parliament. In Great Britain parliament is nearly always in session; in Canada the session is usually over in June. In Great Britain there is a rule of the house that twenty days of each session, that is the winter session, shall be set aside for the unrestricted discussion of estimates, and during those twenty days, which are not consecutive, the opposition is given considerable latitude in the selection of the votes to be criticised. The evolution, as nearly as I can follow it, of the committee on estimates in Great Britain is that it has ceased to function with regard to reporting to the house with respect to the estimates of any particular department in any particular session, but has evolved rather along the lines of trying to

cover in its investigations all departments successively, reaching the same department again in a period of about four to five years, and making an exhaustive examination of each department, its manner of preparing estimates, suggestions of economies which might be developed, but not discussing matters of policy at all.

speechtext:
Practically the same.
Some of the discussions in the British house of which I have record indicate considerable debate as to conflict of jurisdiction between the ordinary auditing arrangments of the government and the functions of this committee. On the whole, however, there appears in Great Britain to be an opinion that the estimates committee-and I am inclined to think it now has the wrong name; it is not strictly speaking an estimates committee in the sense in which we are discussing the matter to-day.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: It does not consider the supply bill until the money has been expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: As my hon. friend says, it does not consider the supply bill until after the money has been expended. But it has evolved rather a-

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: The same as our public accounts committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I wish my hon. friends would allow me to proceed, as I have not much time left. It has evolved into a committee of the house having for its function the examination continuously of the detail operations of the departments of the government, with power to call the officers of those departments before it from time to time, and to report to the government its observations upon the economics of the public service. That is really what the British estimates committee has evolved into, and therefore it is a different thing from what is contemplated in this resolution. I do suggest, however, that this experience on the part of the British parliament points at least to the desirability from our point of view of having the committee on standing orders carefully consider what rules should be adopted for the committees pro-

posed in the resolution now under discussion before we are called upon to extend powers to committees to deal with the estimates.
I merely give this rather sketchy information in order to indicate my belief that a careful study by the committee on standing orders of the operation of this sort of thing elsewhere is desirable before the rules of this house are amended in regard to the matter.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: Are the functions of the committee in the British house which have been described not entirely covered by our committee known as the public accounts committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Perhaps I can best answer the question by reading what I refrained from reading before, the regulations under which the regular estimates committee was established in the British house:
1.	That an estimates committee of eighteen should be appointed.
2.	That the danger of considerable overlapping of functions rendered it undesirable that the estimates committee should sit as a separate body in addition to the select committee on national expenditure and the public accounts committee, and it is therefore proposed that the estimates committee and the select committee on national expenditure should be merged into one.
3.	That in accordance with the procedure that has been adopted in the past in the case of the select committee on national expenditure there should be one committee only but power should be given to it to appoint subcommittees.
4.	That as in other cases of committees whose functions continue from session to session, e.g., the public accounts committee, the same members, as far as may be possible, should be appointed to serve each session, and leave should be given to the committee to sit during adjournments of the house if they so desire.
5.	That the committee should have no power to deal with questions of policy or to advocate increased expenditure. Their functions should be to examine estimates in the light of the government's policy with a view to discovering any possible economies and any items which appeared to involve or to have involved wasteful or unnecessary expenditure or seemed likely to lead to large increases of expenditure in future years.
6.	That the procedure in the House of Commons in regard to supply should remain unaltered and that on the appointment of the estimates committee no hard-and-fast rules should be laid down with the object of securing the postponement of discussions on estimates in committee of supply pending the receipt of reports from the estimates committee. Rules of this character might create serious difficulties in regard to the business of the house and might also lead, in some cases, to hurried and insufficient consideration of the estimates by the committee itself. It is suggested, therefore, that it should be left to the government, in arranging the order in which the estimates are to be discussed in the

Rules oj the House-Mr. Dunning
house, to bear constantly in mind the proceedings of the estimates committee with a view to meeting the convenience both of the committee and the house as far as possible. If it should be found subsequently that some alteration in procedure was desirable, any necessary change could he made in the light of the experience gained by the committee.
7.	That there should be attached to the committee an experienced member of the staff of the House of Commons, whose function it would be to prepare material for the committee's deliberations and to render advice and assistance to the committee and the chairman in particular. Being a servant of the House of Commons, this official would occupy an independent position in relation to ministers.
8.	That this official should not be empowered to call for information from government departments except on the instructions of the chairman of the committee, nor have the right of access to departmental papers, but the committee shall have the ordinary right of sending for persons, papers and records.
9.	That no further staff should be appointed at the present time, and that the committee should decide by experience whether the creation of any additional staff was required.
10.	That the selection of the chairman should be left to the committee.
Now, those were the original regulations under which that committee was established-

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: What is the date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
In 1921-and the committee has been functioning for a number of years. I can best illustrate its evolution by quoting from volume VI of the reports of the committee, page 282 of the records of the British Blouse of Commons. Under head 16 I find the following:
We, are, however, not satisfied with the existing procedure.
This was after a period of years of experience.
We, therefore, recommend that the number [DOT]of members of the estimates committee should be increased next year, which would enable it to subdivide itself into sufficient sub-committees to examine the whole estimates every year. For this purpose we assume that each sub-committee would examine two or three classes according to size, including the revenue departments and fighting services. The reports of the subcommittees would come up for approval by the main committee as at present. As the work *would be onerous and detailed, we further suggest that members of this committee should he excused from service on all private bill committees, and also, if they so desire, on standing committees.
At page 315 of the same volume will be found the ruling of the Lords of the Treasury on the recommendation which I have just read. This is the ruling:
The government do not see their way to adopt the recommendations as to the future size and composition of the committee. It .appears to them that the committee should aim
at reviewing a group of estimates each year so as to cover the full field every four or five years and should endeavour as far as possible to complete this review before the particular group are finally disposed of in supply. This they consider the committee should be able to do without additional members or special facilities.
Since the date of that report, the committee in Great Britain has evolved along these lines, and now -the committee simply takes the estimates of a department as the basis of an investigation of the affairs of that department, and then submits to the treasury, or to the government-the Lords of the Treasury meaning, in this case, the government-for the advice and information of the government when they prepare the estimates for the next fiscal year. The treasury, under the British system, is at liberty either to accept or to reject those suggestions, but as the corrre-spondence is made a public document, the members of the house have the information before them. I have read the textbook by Mr. Durel'l, who is possibly one of the best authorities on this phase of British parliamentary practice. He is quite critical of the work of the estimates committee, but I do not think I can, with advantage, place his views before the house at this stage. They can be easily secured by any member from the library.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: I would like to be perfectly clear on one point, that no matter what is referred to this committee it will not silence or prevent any private member from asking questions or discussing matters when they come down to the committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: As I suggested, Mr. Speaker, that is one of the features which the committee on standing orders would have to consider when the rules were being changed, or the rules of the house amended, to make provision for this procedure. I stated that I did not think that any member of the house would want to preclude members from asking questions, or from discussing estimates in committee of supply.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I thought I heard the
Prime Minister say something to that effect.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before
the house contemplates the setting up o:f a special committee to consider estimates for the current year, that is, estimates that might be referred to such a committee. All estimates, alike in Great Britain and here, are submitted with a message, and the government of the day, being responsible for the raising of the necessary revenues of the country,

Rules of the House-Mr. Bennett
must, in the final analysis, assume the responsibility for the expenditure. All a committee could do would be to examine into the circumstances under which an estimate was made. It could not determine the question of policy, and it certainly could not lessen the estimate, neither could it increase it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
That is perfectly clear.
I was under the impression at one time-and I see that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is of .the same mind with respect to it-that this committee in the English House of Commons had wider power than it in fact has, and he and I discussed the matter with one of the British ministers at one time for the purpose of ascertaining what the powers of that committee were. In this country, the only effect that I can see of such a committee being set up, would be, (a) to enable the committee to ascertain the circumstances under which a given estimate appeared in the estimates; (b) to determine whether or not the amount indicated would be sufficient for the purpose of meeting the proposed expenditure; and (c) any other circumstances that might be relevant to such an inquiry. But it could not deal, as I have said, with either a question of policy, nor yet could it lessen or increase the estimate.
Under the circumstances, the only utility of such a committee would be to save the time of this house, and that would involve the taking of the notes of evidence, the printing of them, and the submitting of them to all the members of this house, in order that they might read them and govern themselves on the circumstances before the estimate came up in the committee of supply. I confess that at various times I have looked into the matter, hoping that there might be some real merit in what I had always believed to be the committee on estimates in Great Britain, in its application to this country, but after I had made the inquiry, which the right hon. the Prime Minister is aware of, I made further inquiries in Great Britain, and also looked at some of the textbooks to which the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has referred, and frankly, the only purpose that would be served by such a committee would be that which I have just indicated, so far as I could ascertain from the study which I gave to the matter.
However, I am bound to say that the committee which was merged with it-the public accounts committee-did serve a useful purpose in Great Britain, and one which I think our public accounts committees should now be willing to undertake. For instance, Great

Britain operates a dockyard at Portsmouth, and I was amazed on one occasion to see the extent to which that committee went into detailed expenditures for the purpose of seeing how public moneys could, in the future, be saved because of what they believed to be excessive expenditures in connection with the payment of wages, and matters of that kind. For instance, suppose we applied that to this country, and had an inquiry before the public accounts committee that would not be partisan in its character-if that is possible before such a committee-as to the expenditures in the Sorel shipyard-and I use that as an illustration because it is a point at which we carry on operations not dissimilar in character to the operations carried on at the Portsmouth dockyard-or in Great Britain where they have many inquiries as to the expenditure in operating the national telephone system. Here we have set up a special committee for the purpose of making inquiries with respect to our national railway system. That special committee is a committee that makes very detailed inquiries as to projected expenditures, but it can serve no great purpose, for this reason, that the estimate of the minister has been made upon the recommendation of the officials before it goes to the committee, and all the committee can do is merely to record-and it always does-its acquiescence in the action of the minister, based on the recommendation of the mangement. What is really necessary, if we are going to deal with that at all, is that there should be an antecedent inquiry before the estimate is made, because once the officials of the railway make their recommendation, and the cabinet accepts it, it is generally assumed that they have given it the best consideration possible, with respect to the recommendations and with respect to the expenditure. I might cite, for example, the case of the Montreal terminals last year. Some of us thought that further inquiries might be desirable or necessary. The government had before it all the information it was possible to have, to enable it to determine whether or not the recommendations made by the railway officials should or should not be made effective, and in the light of the information, given the government concluded to give effect to the recommendations of the officials, and placed in the estimates the necessary money to enable the undertaking to commence.
Now, the idea, I take it, that is in the mind of the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas), is as to whether or not an antecedent inquiry might not be possible so that the recommendations made by officials might be tested by the committee, and the government would have the advantage of the testing

Rules of the House-Mr. Bennett
of those recommendations by a committee to enable it to determine whether or not the expenditures should be made. The question in the minds of some of us at least, was whether or not it was possible, in a country where you have expenditures on the basis we have in this country, to set up a committee on estimates that could adequately deal with the situation, with the constitutional limitations imposed upon it. I am bound to say, in the light of the knowledge I have, and the information I have, it places me greatly in doubt.
That is as far as I am prepared to go, but I might add one word. I do believe that in the interests of parliamentary government the public accounts committee might more adequately discharge a very important duty to the Dominion if it carried on its investigations, not because one party or the other suggests this or the other thing, but in order that a great spending department should have its entire accounts, as set out in the Auditor General's report, considered by that committee, as a group of business men dealing with expenditures from every angle and determining to what extent they might make recommendations in order to ensure a greater return for the money expended. That is certainly a principle that governs in the operations of that committee's work in England. As I have said, not wishing to repeat myself, they have gone into great detail in some of the recommendations they have made. I have felt, more particularly in recent years, that with the great volume of business this country transacts, as indicated by the Auditor General's report, the greatest service that could be rendered by a member or members of this house would be to take an active interest in the public accounts committee, not swayed by the desire to protect ministerial responsibility, but for the purpose of ensuring the greatest possible efficiency in the discharge of the obligations that rest upon the government in regard to the expenditure of public revenues. The very recommendations read from Mr. Durell's book by the Minister of Finance would involve, if applied here, that the committee on public accounts at the beginning of a new parliament would consist, as far as possible, of members who take an interest in matters of that kind, and that so far as possible continuity should be preserved during the lifetime of that parliament in the membership of the committee, and that it would take up from year to year one department of the public service, and dispose not only of the question of expenditures, but deal also with questions of revenue. I urge that,
because at the moment there is no audit of revenues in this country; there is no supervision by the Auditor General of the revenues of Canada at this moment. In the very nature of things that would become exceedingly difficult and is surrounded by many limitations that would be necessarily imposed upon an auditor in connection with the revenues that are derived from operations of the public service. But I submit, and I think the Minister of Finance will find, in the end, that it might serve a great purpose if the public accounts committee were constituted as I have suggested with power preserved during the lifetime of the parliament to take up at the beginning of each session, and to determine national revenue, for instance, under the headings of (a) sources of revenue and (b) checks upon those sources. Then take up the expenditures, as to the circumstances under which they are made, the methods controlling them and take up definitely as the committee does in England the whole operations of that department. Then recommendations could be made to the house and to the government that would enable the government to check revenues more closely and to supervise expenditures in the department to a greater extent.
For instance, there is great overlapping in the public service of this country which is being prevented in England by the work of this committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: To some extent, only.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
It has not attained perfection, of course, but the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury in England exercise a power comparable to that of the Auditor General of this country on the one hand and of the Minister of Finance on the other. I submit that such a committee with authority to exercise that power would be able to ascertain this question. As an illustration, why should four governmental departments be buying the same kind of article, instead of buying through a central purchasing department? Why should a tender be called for a dredge, in one instance by the Minister of Railways and Canals, and another tender be called by the Minister of Public Works for a similar machine? Why should the question of specifications with regard to these matters not have the same form, or shall I say uniformity, so as to provide under conditions familiar to all of us the interchange of parts and the difficulties that arise because of repairs.
It is not this administration only, but if any of the hon. members of this house will take the trouble to look into the public

Rules oj the House-Mr. Bennett
accounts and see the goods that are purchased by each department he will realize what I meant when I used the word "overlapping". Knowing, as I do, the business propensities of the Minister of Finance, I am ,perfectly certain he would say that in the management of a great enterprise he would not permit departmental heads to overlap one another in the operations of their respective departments. I think that is clear. How is it to be dealt with? Certainly the committee on estimates would not be able to accomplish a reform in that direction. But I repeat that my own study of the constitution convinces me that if the members of this house who come here with the desire to do useful public service and find difficulty in performing that service would go up to the public accounts committee at the beginning of a new parliament and have it understood that continuity is being maintained as far as possible in the work of that committee, and take up the operations of one department of public service in the first year, and see it through in the way in which it is done by the committee in Great Britain to which reference was made, they would do as great a service for this country as it is possible for members of parliament to do. In that way they could make recommendations as to how we would be able to supervise and make effective and efficient expenditures of public money, while ensuring every available dollar of revenue. I say that in the light of the study I have been ablf to devote to this matter. I say it to the committee of this house with some hesitancy, because I had thought at one time it fight be possible for this committee on eetim, as to attain a wider and greater result than I know now to be possible under the constitutional limitations imposed upon the expenditure of public money.
One word more, and I 'have concluded. There is no reason why we should not in the light of what the right hon. the Prime Minister has been good enough to say as to the attitude of the government, instead of changing the rules, refer the estimates of some small spending department to a select standing committee that we could name. There is no reason why we should not try it out, authorizing to every member the right to attend the committee and the right to ask such questions as he might think desirable in order that the complete record might be prepared. It would be understood, just as in the case of the special committee dealing with the national railways, that such committee would have its proceedings printed, ana every

member of the house would have the opportunity to read and study them before the estimates of that department were under consideration by the committee of supply.
Of course, the observations by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) must prevail, as the right hon. t'he Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance indicated, namely, that that should not be taken as in any sense curbing the right of inquiry or investigation, or the night to question the minister himself when the estimates are under consideration by the committee.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
The reason for this resolution, as my friend remarked, and as I understand the sense and spirit of it and the motive which prompted the resolution, was that private members of this house might be able to get better and speedier in-formatiou in connection with the estimates. It has been a remarkable feature to me, as a member of this house for four years, to note the speed with which these estimates go through. Sometimes when we get to estimates the chairman of the committee calls for a vote before we have had time to read the figures; my hon. friends opposite say "Carried, carried", and we have carried millions of dollars in a few minutes. When information was wanted it was found that although the minister and the deputy minister both were there it was almost impossible to obtain it..
Therefore, I consider that the principle of this resolution, however it may be carried out, would enable us to pass these estimates intelligently and not vote millions of dollars in a few minutes. These estimates could be referred to some committee where not only the deputy minister but the engineers and officers of the department would be present, and full information could be obtained. It has been the experience in the past that when the house began to get a little weary and eleven o'clock was being reached, estimates have passed through without any consideration being given to them or without any information being offered as to the requirements of the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES

If the experience of the British house is to be any guide, they will pass much more quickly than is now the case.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES

But with more information being obtained.
