In speaking to the subject of the resolution itself and without going into the further field indicated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), there would appear to be a need for a great deal of study in this direction. Two benefits are suggested in the resolution; one is that the house would have further information, and the other is that it would save the time of the house. Like other members of the house, when estimates are being considered I realize how impossible it is to obtain information, and how much we are working in the dark. As has already been pointed out, the adoption of this proposal simply would mean that a few members would have fuller information, and unless the proceedings of the commitees were published and circulated the other members of the house would not have that advantage.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
When the estimates were
before the house those members who possessed that information would be able to carry on a more intelligent discussion and impart to the other members what information they possessed.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
That is quite possible, but
still the great majority of the members would be brought face to face with certain estimates without having the knowledge possessed by the few.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: Why does the hon. member suggest that there would be only a few members on that committee? What is to prevent every member of the house being on such a committee?

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
If every member of the
house were on that committee we might just as well continue as at present. There might be possibly some advantage in having even a few members of the house fully informed as to the details of any particular item and of the circumstances under which it appeared in the estimates.
As to the saving of time, I doubt very much whether that would be accomplished. Complaint has been made that we pass the estimates too hurriedly, but that argument and the argument that we would be saving time do not fit together. I think hon. members of the house will agree that time is not wasted- perhaps that is not the proper word. Time is hot unnecessarily consumed in discussing such items as appear in the estimates. The great proportion of the time consumed in discussing estimates is taken up with items which do not appear therein. That has been the experience of previous years as well as during the present year when the estimates of the Minister of Public Works have been considered. Of course, I do not dispute that hon. members have a perfect right to criticize the non-appearance of certain items.
I cannot see that the adoption of this proposal would lessen in any way the amount of time spent by the house in the discussion of these matters.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much pleased with the attitude taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon, and before I close I intend to move an amendment along the lines suggested by him.
I was interested in the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mt. Bennett), and in looking up the debate upon the resolution introduced in 1925 I find that I expressed somewhat the same opinion. I said:
T drafted this resolution last year before I left the house and if I were preparing it to-day I would make the suggested change a little more sweeping than is proposed here. I think possibly the time to cut down estimates is before they are printed and given to the house, and it might be advisable for us to have a committee on estimates who would go over the estimates of the deputy ministers before they were printed and submitted to parliament.
I do not think it would be possible to get the house to adopt anything as sweeping as that, but I think it would be better if the public accounts committee examined the estimates of t'he Public Works department before rather than after the money was spent. I was a member of that committee for many years, and I remember one occasion when we discussed for three weeks the expenditure which had been made on a small harbour in western Ontario. I imagine that the cost of operating the committee for that length of time equalled the amount which had been spent upon the harbour.
I am going to suggest to the Prime Minister that a start be made this year with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. Those estimates usually take up from one to three weeks of the time of the house, and if they were taken up before the agriculture committee those members who are particularly interested in agriculture could attend and obtain the information which we have never

Rules oj the House-Mr. Jacobs
been able to obtain in the house. It might be that the heads of the department could obtain some ideas from the committee which would enable them to give the country better value for the money expended.
I do not think there would be very much time saved, but it is possible there might be a little. This is only an experiment which we are making, and it might be conducted along similar lines to the procedure followed with the estimates of the Canadian National Railway. I would prefer to make use of our select standing committees; I do not like to urge the government to establish additional committees because that would likely cause confusion when the different committees tried to meet at convenient times.
I do not want to take up the time of the house any further, because I think the resolution has met with a very favourable reception. I will dose simply by moving the following amendment:
That the resolution be amended by inserting the word "certain" in place of the word "the" in the second line thereof and by inserting the words "or a special committee" after the word "committees" in the second line thereof.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to declare at the outset -that I am in favour of the resolution of the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas). I believe this is the first time that I have ever agreed with him, and I am beginning to ask myself whether I am right or not. The resolution, however, on the face of it appears to be -perfectly innocent and there seem to me to be many features about it which ought to appeal to the house. I consider the change, if adopted, is one which will make for efficiency, thoroughness and a saving of time, all of which I think are necessary even in this House of Commons. For the last- fourteen- years I have been present when the estimates have been brought before the house, and everyone admits that there is room for a good deal of improvement. First of all, I do not thinik, speaking in a general way, the ministers are as efficient or as thorough as they ought to be.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: We are agreed o-n that.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: I have been here since 1917 so that I know both sides and I do not think one side is very much of an improvement over the other.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext: My hon. friend holds up the present administration as an example.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I think they are just "run
of mine"-the hon. member for Richmond-

West Cape Breton will understand what that is-and I do not see very much improvement in the offing. Very often a minister who takes charge of the estimates is a new man who does not know very much about the department. Sometimes he is pitchforked in very suddenly, and often he is one of the most surprised of men when he finds himself in the position. He has to lean upon the official who comes here with the estimates. Questions are asked of the minister; he does not know what answer to make; a whispered conversation takes place between him and the official who is sometimes the deputy minister, sometimes the assistant to the deputy and sometimes an aide to the assistant; a discussion goes on between them and finally some kind of answer is supplied. It may not satisfy the committee, and the minister, if h-e happens to be a diplomat, will tell the committee: I shall be able to give my hon. friend the information he wants to-morrow. Then the storm blows over and the minister is allowed to go on for a little while longer. Why should we not send these estimates to a committee which would have the right of examining not only the officer himself who is providing the information for the minister, but those who prepared the estimates? I do not see why the entire house should not be on that committee if the house wishes to be on it. They can sit in the morning; the house can sit in the ordinary way in the afternoon and the evening, and we would1 be having a sort of two-ringed performance. Those who are interested in the estimates can sit in the committee, and those who are interested in divorces and other matters can sit in the house. In that way there would be some variety. I often think, when I hear a question being asked of a minister and observe his inability to answer it, the proper answer being really that of the deputy, it is very much like the ancient story of Balaam's ass: The minister is asked a question and the deputy answers it. All this would be avoided by the suggestion made by the bon. member for Camrose. We would have the right to summon before us the persons we want with the papers, and then everyone would be satisfied.
Moreover there would not be such grandstand play in the committee. Here we are talking to the whole of Canada. We have the entire press listening, taking down what we 'have to say, and the next morning every man expects to find himself famous. We shall do away with that. We do not want that kind of thing, and we shall have more efficiency in the work. Being one of the

Rules of the House-Mr. Evans
oldest members, I have seen time and time again in the house trouble develop 'between a member on one side and a member on the other on a purely personal matter. They call each other all the names which parliamentary procedure will allow and sometimes they go a little beyond it. The matter has nothing whatever to do with the estimates before the house, but they ventilate their grievance. We are considering an estimate, say for the building of a harbour, and before that is allowed to pass, some hon. gentleman on the other side-always on the other side, of course-will get up and want to know why a postmaster's son was dismissed five years ago from a certain department. Then the whole question will shift to the dismissal of the postmaster's son and we shall have two or three hours' discussion on that or the dismissal of the postmaster himself or the postmaster's sister or something of that kind. The serious work we have on hand is diverted when we go in for a discussion of that sort. Such a procedure is not creditable to parliament and it should not be allowed to continue. We know the weakness of the system and we propose to change it, I think very much for the better.
There are many of us who are not interested in some particular estimates which are before the house. I never could work up much enthusiasm over the estimates for repairs to coves and breakwaters in Nova Sootia, and yet we have had to sit here night after night listening to discussions on such matters.

speechtext: Yes, but the bloom would be off the peach. Lightning never strikes twice in the same place. When a question has been thoroughly discussed and hon gentlement have called each other all the names they like in a committee, they are not going to come back to the house and repeat the performance here. We cannot play any return engagement, particularly on the estimates, so that altogether I am strongly in favour of the resolution. I think it is high time that we had it. Most of these estimates pass through leisurely until towards the end of the session, and then what happens? On a single night we will pass twenty or twenty-five millions of dollars. We do not know what it is all about, but we are anxious to catch the five o'clock or the eleven o'clock train. We are patriotic so long as we know that the train is not waiting in the station, but when we know it is waiting we lose our patriotism and leave other people to canyon the work. That is not as it should be. If the estimates came before a special committee or a select standing committee, every item would be discussed, and if they were not properly discussed there they would be when they came before the committee of the whole. The entire estimates would have a thorough overhauling in the special or select standing committee, where those interested would have the particular ones in which they were interested ventilated, and finally they would come here to be touched up and made ready for passing in the regular way. I am therefore strongly in favour of this resolution, and although it is proposed by my hon. friend from Camrose, I hope it will be supported nevertheless.

speechtext:
The
motive behind this motion is to secure more information regarding the expenditure of large sums of public money. It has always been a mystery to me what has been the motive behind certain projects. I think that more careful scrutiny should be made of the expenditure of large sums of money in certain places. I would point, for instance, to the elevator that has been built on Vancouver island for the storage of western grain. Why it was ever built there is beyond our comprehension. There seems to be no reason for it; we are under the necessity of ferrying the grain across, and our own national railway system is put to greater expense on that account. If we could have all the estimates brought before a body such as could be appointed by this house there would be a more careful scrutiny made of such expenditures, and greater care would be exercised in allotting large sums of money for such projects. I believe that we should at least give this plan a trial. I am heartily in favour of the motion.

speechtext:
I
take it that the object of this resolution is not necessarily to out down or increase the estimates, but merely that we may secure proper information before a committee where we would have access to the technical officers of the department concerned, and in the light of that information the passing of the estimates through the house would be facilitated.
Regarding the question which has been raised that the work of such a committee would preclude discussion in the house, may I point out that no one is precluded from asking questions in the house simply because the estimate in question has been before a committee. I would point out that all members of the house are permitted to attend the sittings of a committee. The fact that I do not belong to a particular committee does not bar me from attending and hearing the discussion and asking questions if necessary, or asking one of the members of the committee to ask a question for me if I am precluded from doing so myself. I think, therefore, that there should be no objection on that score. However, I would not be in favour of presenting these estimates to one particular committee, as has been suggested here today. I think that the different estimates should be submitted to the committee dealing with that particular business, that the agricultural estimates, for instance, should be submitted to the committe on agriculture. I take it that most of the members of that committee are men who are primarily interested in agriculture, otherwise they would not be on that committee, and these are the men who would be most likely to ask for information on those estimates in the house. Instead of taking up the time of the house, they can ask their questions in the committee of the officers of the department, instead of bothering the minister, who probably has not the technical knowledge to enlighten them. We have a precedent already in the railway committee, which is a special committee of this house appointed to deal with Canadian National railway estimates. So really there is no new departure proposed. It is simply extending a principle that has already been accepted.
There is another reason, and a very important one, why I am in favour of this resolution, and that is that for some reason or other which is hard to understand there is less partisan spirit in the committees than in the house. Perhaps it is because we are seated differently; perhaps because when I attend a meeting of a committee I might find myself, for instance, sitting next to my genial friend from Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). We would not quarrel in a committee as we might across

the floor of this house. There is no party organization in a committee, and I think that is the main reason-party organization certainly has something to do with it. We are sitting here in different groups, and I think we are sometimes actuated by our respective positions. I think that these estimates could be dealt with much better and more efficiently and more information be secured by a committee than in the house.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO SELECT COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I am very glad indeed to witness the reception which the resolution moved by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) has met with in the house. I am glad to note that both the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) as well as different ministers of the crown, have spoken in favour of this proposal.
I am not going to kill the resolution with kindness by extending my remarks, but I wish to say that while I am in favour of this resolution, I am not satisfied with it; I would like to see it go much further. Some hon. members who have spoken have emphasized that while more accurate information may be obtained in a committee under the method proposed here than it is possible to obtain in committee of the whole, it will be impossible for the committee to increase or decrease any particular estimate even if the intelligence of the committee suggested the desirability of such action. I know that to alter the estimates in that way would be interfering with the present practice under our parliamentary system, but that is what I want to do; I want to interfere with it. If this thing called democracy is to have any practical meaning, the members of this house must get control of the expenditure and not leave it in the hands of the cabinet. However, that is not implied in the resolution itself. I am merely stating that while I am glad to see the resolution go as far as it does, it does not go far enough for me, and I hope that in the years to come some hon. member will push that fight to a successful conclusion.

speechtext:
If the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) would permit me, I would like to express my hearty endorsation of the attitude which he takes on this question. I thought his logic was perfect when he traced the evolution of the committee in the British House of Commons. As indicated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), it started off with the idea of considering the estimates. Before it had gone very far it found itself amalgamated with practically the committee on public accounts. Then after some years experience they found

Rules oj the House-Mr. Neill
it was not functioning in the way it was designed to function and they started another kind of policy; instead of looking through the estimates every year they took a certain section and got round to that section once in four or five years. That is certainly a doctrine entirely different from what is suggested here. Then it evolved until it got down to the proposal recommended by the hon. leader of the opposition, that simply greater attention should be paid to the work of the public accounts committee, which has always been very slightly attended, and which has great possibilities even under our rules to-day. He pointed out very truly that this proposed committee, as indicated by the resolution, would have no real power, and that if it was going to have any power it should be dealing with estimates before they are prepared, that after they have received the endorsation of the engineer, the minister, and the treasury department and have been brought down to the house, any comment made in committee would be just as futile as it is when made in the house, with the exception that we would not have the advantage of making our complaints public, because the meeting would be held in a more or less Star Chamber manner, without Hansard being present; and as the hon. leader of the opposition pointed out, we could not add to those estimates, we could not take from them, we could only do exactly what we are doing here, and it would be simply an unnecessary burden. Surely once is enough to wade through these estimates every session.
My hon. friend from Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) dwelt very fully on a certain feature, and some other hon. members took the same line, but their statements are mutually contradictory of each other. The one hon. gentleman would say, "Let us pass this; it would save the time of the house." My friend took that line. He said we could blow off our steam in committee and would not have to do it here. Another hon. member said, "You are not going to lose any of your privileges, you will have the same chance to ventilate your grievances as you have now." Then what is the use of a duplication of what is already admitted to be a long drawn out and tedious performance? It will be rather longer and we will have it all over again in this house. What shall it profit a man if we do that? I agree with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) who opposed the idea that the items would go through so much easier because the house would be informed. But that is the trouble, it will be only the members of a small committee that will be informed, and the member, the interests of whose constituents are at
stake, is not going to be satisfied because some man sitting on his own or the other side thinks it is all right. Only the man vitally interested knows about the particular item, and he is going to talk about it sooner or later when it comes down to this house.
Now, I might briefly dealy with some of the points which have been brought up to-day, and which I see I dealt with somewhat fully last session. It has been said to-day several times, and pointed to as an illustration, what an advantage it was to have the estimates of the national railways referred to a committee, and how well it worked. Yes, my hon. friend from St. John and Albert (Mr. MacLaren), I think it was, pointed out how it really worked; that we no longer knew the first thing about those estimates-we in this house who are not on that particular small committee. We never hear those estimates discussed now, and after all we, the big body of parliament, are supremely ignorant of what those estimates are. The estimates are called, and if anybody does make inquiries the minister hastens to say, "This was fully discussed in the committee;" and then we are supposed to accept that statement. It is suggested that the same procedure would be an advantage in handling these other estimates; but there is this material and great difference between the two. I may quote:
The Canadian National Railway estimates represent what is entirely a national proposition. Broad policies are discused, you have Sir Henry Thornton and his staff in attendance, and the leaders of the various groups in the house can readily agree whether the policy is a good one or not. But the other estimates are local estimates and so to speak, specialized; think of the thousand and one items that comprise the agricultural estimates, or those of the marine and fisheries or the Post Office Department-almost any of the estimates in fact other than the larger ones in connection with the national railways. Those items require local knowledge to illuminate them, as it were. As you know, the procedure now is for the minister to explain the reason for the estimate from the book that is placed in front of him If further information is required, perhaps the over-burdened memory of the deputy minister is drawn on; but in the last analysis when it comes down to the giving of information for or against that particular item, is it not the member for the local district whose particular knowledge is relied on, and in the special committee that local knowledge will be lacking except as it may be furnished by the few members composing the committee.
Owing to the necessity of having members available for other committees, this committee would be a small one. Indeed, the tendency under the rules passed a couple of years ago is to make our committtees smaller and stilll smaller which I think is a mistake. Those four or five, or a dozen, men if you
Rules of the House-Mr. Neill

like, are going to advise and give opinions on matters about which they are entirely ignorant. An item may relate to some place three or four thousand miles away, but to one member of that committee is to be entrusted the duty of getting the item through. The committee cannot rely upon the assistance of the member that represents the district, I do not care on which side of the house he sits. That is one of the essential objections to this principle, and I submit that my remarks fully meet the argument that this proposal is in any way similar to the reference of the Canadian National estimates to a special committee.
The next item to which I wish to draw attention is that the results of these proceedings will be that the overworked minister- because he is busy at this time of the year; try and see any of them and you will find that to be the case-and his equally overworked deputy, who also is very busy, shall be compelled to go over their estimates twice, once in the sessional committee-shall I call it the hole-and-corner committee?-and again on the floor of this house. What use will it be to anybody if the work is done twice? The answer again will be that it will shorten debate in the house. But will it? Allow me to quote again:
That is all right, sir, as regards the estimates of the Canadian National Railways. When the three leaders in this house and the outstanding members of their parties tell us in committee of the whole, "We have looked at these estimates of the Canadian National Railways and are satisfied with them," I for one am quite prepared to accept their view, as I have no doubt are other members. But, as I say, the conditions are totally different with respect to what I call the local estimates. When it comes down to local matters affecting the coal mining, farming, logging and fishing interests of the constituency which I represent, I say emphatically, no; I will not surrender my right to discuss these matters; I will not surrender it to any lawyer from Winnipeg, any millionaire from Toronto, or any business man from Halifax, however worthy they may be; however much abler they are than I am in their particular spheres, they do not know the local conditions of the district I represent. I know that the time honoured gag will be trotted out: "Oh. but you can go before the committee and vcu will be allowed to speak there." How often have I not heard that advanced: You can go to the committee although you are not a member of it and you will be accorded a courteous hearing. Yes, you will be given a courteous hearing once; but when it comes down to butting in-to use a common expression-on every item and arguing the merits and taking an active part generally in the debate you will soon find that you are not wanted. Any member butting in- I cannot use any other word to express the idea 

will find that he has as much weight there as the Hansard reporter has in the debates that take place in this chamber.

There is a great deal in* that that we will be precluded from furnishing the local information which alone the local member
possesses.

I then come to a point that has been dealt with by several members, and that is the advantages that will accrue to us by expediting the proceedings in this chamber, and then we will be able to go home earlier. I think I have indicated my belief that it would save no time at all, for the reasons that I have given. But suppose it does save time. I would submit to the house in all seriousness that there are greater advantages by our considering every item in committee of the whole, than by getting through quickly and going home, which is the main bait held out in this case. There are a good many members of this house, myself amongst them-and I am not ashamed to admit it-who exhibited great anxiety to come here and occupy the honourable position we hold, and who by hard-fought campaigns and many promises, secured this much sought boon. We told the people that we would do our duty to the last ditch, and so forth. Now 2419-35
are we getting tired and lazy? Do we want to shirk the obligations which we undertook when we came here? A few days, a week or two longer, would not make any great difference. I would point out also, to put it bluntly, that we are being paid for being here. I admit that the salary is quite incommensurate with the work we do, but at the same time we knew what the remuneration was when we sought the position, and if we are not satisfied to do the work for which we were sent here, we should resign. I know there are scores of men in the district I represent fully as able and quite as willing to represent my constituency.
Another time-honoured gag will be trotted out for our delectation. When the report comes from the select private committee, we shall be told: "Now this matter has been seriously and carefully-almost prayerfully-considered in the select committee and the house would be well advised to accept their just and wise verdict". Let any member of the house try to have a change made in the report of a select committee. The answer would be advanced that this thing has been thoroughly discussed in committee much better than we can discuss it. And it is an argument that has a great deal of weight with a great many hon. gentlemen. Last year I gave an illustration of where I had an important amendment -at least I thought it was-to put into something that was coming through one of those committees, and I thought I had lined it up so that I would be able to carry the thing. It was a small committee, and one of the friends whom I was counting on did not turn up, and the motion was lost. I met him the following da}r and reproached him with his absence. He said he was very sorry but he had gone to have his hair cut; and because that hon. gentleman had gone to have his hair cut, something of material importance to certain interests in the country had to stand over for another year. That is the effect of accepting always the report of a small select standing committee. They say, it went to a committee and we must sustain the committee; in the same way it is popular to say we must sustain the Speaker.
I come to another point, and one of considerable importance. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has been quite conspicuous, and I think properly so, in dealing with the question of divorce for the last two or three years in this house. As we all know, he began his campaign by dwelling upon the way these divorces were railroaded through, without the slightest attention being paid to them in this house. There is no question that that is so, Mr. Speaker. We knew it was so, but nothing

I do not wish to go into the question of divorce at all, but what I wanted to illustrate was this-and I think I am perfectly in order-that we have got into this habit of dealing with divorce cases because we trust the report of that committee to which they are referred. As I say, we trust in them; they may study them or they may not, but when they come to this house we accept them as quickly as the clerk can read them out, because we think they have been dealt with by the committee and we do not need to bother with them. We do not bother with them, and that is an example of what may happen if we create the machinery now proposed. We would say, "The committee dealt with this. It looks rather funny and I think I should ask about it, but I suppose it was dealt with by the committee. If it was not dealt with by them it should have been, and I will let it go." That is the way it would happen, and it would end in a duplication of inquiry, or no inquiry at all. No one will say for one moment that divorce cases are handled properly by the slack system we have adopted. I think the Minister of Finance advanced the argument that it would enable us to get through more quickly in that way, but it is open to the objection I have stated.
There is another feature which has not been touched upon this afternoon. It is not a mere question of passing estimates for this post office or that wharf, or something of that character; what is valuable is the discussion that arises out of the estimates. Sometimes, as -my hon, friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) said, at is not what is in the estimates, but what should be in the estimates, that forms the valuable contribution not only to the

knowledge of the house but to the knowledge of the individual members of the ministry. Statements made to cabinet ministers in their offices, or in caucus, if I may refer to them, are almost entirely ex-parte, are they not? But it is in the light of the publicity obtained in this house that the members of the cabinet get the cross current of public sentiment. If they bring down a statement this year, and members of the house show by their attitude that they think it is too much or too little, the ministers have their ears to the ground and say to each other, "The house was a little restive about passing that estimate last year; perhaps we had better not go too strongly on it this year." We had an illustration of that last session, when a private member who sat next to me moved, out o-f a blue sky, that a vote of something like a million dollars should be cut down to one dollar. It was like a bomb shell, especially to the government, and a revelation as to the number of people who inclined to support the amendment. I think the government, being not unintelligent, realized that the sense of the house was generally against any considerable expenditure for assisted immigration. I think the estimates have been framed this year in some regard, with that point of view in mind. If that estimate had been passed in some private committee consisting of five men, my hon. friend perhaps not being one of them, it might have been impossible for the government to get that point of view of public sentiment. If public sentiment is not entitled to make itself heard in the House of Commons, where is it to be heard?
